docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: ​本文​介绍​计算机系统​中​三个​重要​定律​

docs.title: Amdhal Law
docs.text:
• f: Parallelizable fraction of a program
  • N: Number of processors
\[Speedup=\frac{1}{1-f + f/N}\]
  • Serial bottleneck of Amdahl’s Law:
    • Maximum speedup (1/(1-f)) limited by serial portion (1 - f)
  • Parallel portion (f) is usually not perfectly parallel
    • Synchronization overhead (e.g., updates to shared data)
    • Load imbalance overhead (imperfect parallelization)
    • Resource sharing overhead (contention among N processors)
​更​一般​的​说明

docs.title: 1. Amdahl​定律​的​定义
docs.text: Amdahl​定律​指出​：​系统​中​某​一​部件​（​或​功能​）​由于​性能​提升​而​带来​的​系统​整体​性能​改进​，​受限于​该​部件​在​总​执行​时间​中所​占​的​比例​。

docs.title: 2. ​数学公式
docs.text:
​设​：

  • \( T_{\text{old}} \) ​为​改进​前​的​系统​总​执行​时间​。
  • ​改进​部分​在​总​执行​时间​中​的​占​比​为​ \( f \)（0 ≤ f ≤ 1）。
  • ​该​部分​改进​后​的​加速​比​为​ \( s \)（​即​改进​后该​部分​的​执行​时间​变为​原来​的​ \( 1/s \)）。

​那么​改进​后​的​总​执行​时间​ \( T_{\text{new}} \) ​为​：

\[ T_{\text{new}} = T_{\text{old}} \times \left( (1 - f) + \frac{f}{s} \right) \]

​系统​的​整体​加速​比​ \( S \) ​为​：

\[ S = \frac{T_{\text{old}}}{T_{\text{new}}} = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + \frac{f}{s}} \]

​当​ \( s \to \infty \) ​时​，​加速​比​的​极限​为​：

\[ S_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{1 - f} \]

​这​意味着​，​即使​无限​优化​某一​部件​，​整体​性能​提升​也​受限于​不可​优化​部分​ \( 1-f \)。

docs.title: 3. ​局限性​与​注意事项
docs.text:
• Amdahl​定律​假设​改进​部分​可以​独立​优化​，​且​不​考虑​开销​（​如​通信​、​同步​开销​）。​实际​中​，​并行​化会​引入​额外​开销​，​导致​加速​比​低于​理论值​。
  • ​它​只​给出​了​加速​比​的​上限​，​并未​考虑​实现​的​复杂性​。
  • ​在​多任务​系统​中​，​如果​任务​可以​动态​调整​，Amdahl​定律​的​适用性​需要​谨慎​。

docs.title: Roofline Model
docs.text: Roofline​模型​（​屋顶​线​模型​）​是​一种​用于​可视化​和​分析​计算机系统​性能​瓶颈​的​直观​模型​，​旨在​帮助​开发者​理解​应用程序​的​性能​是​受限于​计算能力​（CPU/GPU​的​FLOPS）​还是​内存​带宽​。

docs.title: 1. ​核心​概念​：​运算​强度
docs.text:
Roofline​模型​引入​了​一个​关键​指标​：​运算​强度​Arithmetic Intensity(AI)。

  • ​定义​：​程序​每​读取​或​写入​1​字节​数据​，​需要​进行​多少​次​浮点运算​。

  • ​公式​：

    \[ \text{​运算​强度​} = \frac{\text{​浮点运算​次数​ (FLOPs)}}{\text{​访存​数据量​ (Bytes)}} \]

  • ​单位​：FLOPs/Byte。

​这个​指标​衡量​的​是​计算​的​重用​性​：

  • ​低​运算​强度​：​意味着​程序​每次​从​内​存取数据​后​，​只​进行​少量​计算​（​如​简单​的​向量​加法​）。​这​类​程序​通常​受限于​内存​带宽​，​称为​内存​受限​。
  • ​高​运算​强度​：​意味着​程序​每次​取​数据​后​，​会​进行​大量​计算​（​如​矩阵​乘法​、​深度​学习​卷积​）。​这​类​程序​通常​受限于​CPU/GPU​的​计算能力​，​称为​计算​受限​。

docs.title: 2. ​模型​的​构成
docs.text:
Roofline​模型​是​一个二维​坐标系​图表​，​形似​屋顶​：

  • X​轴​：​运算​强度​ （FLOPs/Byte），​从左到右​递增​（​通常​使用​对数​坐标​）。
  • Y​轴​：​性能​ （GFLOPS/s ​或​ FLOPS/s），​从下到上​递增​。

​图表​中​包含​两条​关键​的​“​线​”​或​“​区域​”：

docs.title: 第一层​：​屋顶​的​斜率​部分​ —— ​带宽​受限​区域
docs.text:
• ​公式​：\( \text{​性能​} = \text{​运算​强度​} \times \text{​内存​带宽​} \)
  • ​解释​：​当​运算​强度​较​低时​，​无论​你​的​计算​核心​有​多​快​，​程序​都​被​“​内存​墙​”​堵住​了​。​性能​主要​取决于​内存​子系统​能​喂给​计算​核心​多少​数据​。​这部分​是​一条​斜率​为​正数​的​直线​（\( y = kx \)）。
  • ​瓶颈​：​内存​带宽​。

docs.title: 第二层​：​屋顶​的​天花板​ —— ​计算​受限​区域
docs.text:
• ​公式​：\( \text{​性能​} = \text{​峰值​计算​性能​} \)
  • ​解释​：​当​运算​强度​足够​高时​，​数据​一旦​取​到​缓存​/​寄存器​中​，​就​能​进行​大量​运算​。​此时​，​性能​不再​受​内存​速度限制​，​而是​受限于​计算​核心​能​有​多​快​。​这部分​是​一条​水平线​（\( y = \text{​常数​} \)）。
  • ​瓶颈​：​计算能力​（FLOPS）。

​两者​的​交点​：​两条线​的​交点​对应​的​运算​强度​称为​“​临界点​”。​当​运算​强度​大于​该​临界点​时​，​程序​进入​计算​受限​区域​。

docs.title: 1. ​识别​性能​瓶颈
docs.text: • ​诊断​：​通过​计算​实际​程序​的​性能​（Y​值​）​和​运算​强度​（X​值​），​将​其​放在​图上​。​如果​它​远​低于​理论​屋顶​线​，​说明​存在​优化​空间​；​如果​它​紧贴​某条线​，​说明​瓶颈​就​在​那里​。

docs.title: 2. ​指导​代码优化
docs.text:
• ​内存​受限​型​：​尝试​循环​分块​（Tiling）、​数据​复用​、​合并​内存​访问​等​。
  • ​计算​受限​型​：​尝试​向​量化​、​增加​并行度​、​使用​更​高效​的​数学​库​。

docs.title: 3. ​评估​硬件​潜力
docs.text: • ​对于​新​架构​，​可以​画出​其​Roofline​图​。​这能​直观​显示​：​对于​给定​的​运算​强度​，​硬件​能​提供​多少​性能​。

docs.title: 4. ​分层​屋顶​（​多​层级​内存​）
docs.text:
​现代​Roofline​模型​往往​不止​一个​屋顶​。​因为​内存​层次结构​（L1​缓存​、L2​缓存​、L3​缓存​、​主存​）​每​一层​都​有​不同​的​带宽​。

  • ​可以​画出​多条​斜线​：L1​带宽​线​、L2​带宽​线​、DRAM​带宽​线​。
  • ​如果​数据​主要​命中​L1​缓存​，​程序​可能​沿着​L1​线​的​斜率​走​；​如果​数据​必须​从​主存​读取​，​则​受限于​DRAM​带宽​线​。
  • ​这​有助于​分析​数据​在​不同​缓存​层次​上​的​停留​情况​。

docs.title: Little's Law
docs.text: Little's Law​是​一个​在​运筹学​、​排队​论​以及​计算机系统​性能​分析​中​非常​基础​的​定律​。

docs.title: 1. ​核心​定义​与​公式
docs.text:
Little's Law​的​表述​非常简单​，​它​适用​于​任何​处于​稳定​状态​（Steady State）​的​系统​。

\[ N = X \times R \]

​其中​：

  • \( N \) （L）：​系统​中​的​平均​请求​/​任务​数​（​例如​：​服务器​中​正在​排队​和​处理​的​平均​HTTP​请求​数量​）。
  • \( X \) （\lambda）：​系统​的​平均​吞吐量​（​例如​：​服务器​每秒​处理​的​请求​数​，​即​ departure rate）。
  • \( R \) （W）：​每个​请求​在​系统​中​的​平均​停留​/​响应​时间​（​例如​：​从​请求​到达​直到​处理​完成​的​平均​耗时​）。

​定律​的​核心思想​：​在​稳定​状态​下​，​系统​中​的​人数​等于​人们​进入​系统​的​速率​乘以​每个​人​在​系统​中​停留​的​时间​。

docs.title: 2. ​直观​理解
docs.text:
​想象​一家​银行​：

  • L（​平均​请求​数​）：​银行​里​平均​有​ \( N \) ​个人​（​包括​正在​办​业务​的​和​排队​的​）。
  • λ（​吞吐量​）：​银行​大门​每分钟​能​进来​ \( X \) ​个人​，​同时​也​能​出去​ \( X \) ​个人​（​假设​平衡​）。
  • W（​响应​时间​）：​每个​人​在​银行​里​待​的​平均​时间​是​ \( R \) ​分钟​。

Little's Law​告诉​我们​：​银行​里​的​人数​ = ​进门​的​速度​ × ​每人​待​的​时间​。

​如果​你​看到​银行​里​总是​挤满​了​人​（\( L \) ​很大​），​要么​是因为​顾客​来得​太快​（\( \lambda \) ​很大​），​要么​是因为​每个​顾客​办​业务​太久​（\( W \) ​很长​）。

docs.title: 3. ​在​计算机系统​中​的​典型​应用
docs.text: Little's Law​在​计算机​性能​工程​中​无处不在​，​特别​是​在​分析​服务器​性能​、​数据库​连接池​、​缓存​系统​时​。

docs.title: 应用​一​：​分析​Web​服务器​性能
docs.text:
​假设​你​有​一个​Web​服务器​：

  • ​你​监控​到​平均​有​ \( N = 100 \) ​个​并发​请求​正在​处理​中​。
  • ​服务器​的​吞吐量​是​ \( X = 2000 \) ​请求​/​秒​。
  • ​问​：​平均​响应​时间​ \( R \) ​是​多少​？

​根据​公式​：

\[ R = \frac{N}{X} = \frac{100}{2000} = 0.05 \text{​秒​} = 50 \text{ms} \]

​这​意味着​，​如果​你​看到​并发​数​很​高​，​同时​吞吐量​很​低​，​那么​响应​时间​必然​很长​。

docs.title: 应用​二​：​容量​规划​与​负载​测试
docs.text:
​在​进行​压力​测试​时​，Little's Law​可以​帮助​验证​测试数据​的​真实性​。

  • ​如果​你​通过​埋点​测得​响应​时间​ \( R \) ​是​100ms，​吞吐量​ \( X \) ​是​1000 QPS。
  • ​那么​理论​上​系统​中​的​并发​请求​数​应为​ \( N = 1000 \times 0.1 = 100 \)。
  • ​如果​你​实际​监控​到​的​并发​线程​数​远大于​或​小于​100，​说明​你​的​测量​可能​有误​，​或者​系统​存在​阻塞​（​如​线程​被​挂​起​但​没有​在​处理​请求​）。

docs.title: 应用​三​：​排队​论​与​多处理器
docs.text:
​在​多​核​处理器​处理​任务​队列​时​：

  • ​如果​有​ \( N \) ​个​任务​在​队列​中​等待​或​被​处理​，CPU​核​的​完成​速率​是​ \( X \)，​那么​每个​任务​等待​和​处理​完成​的​总​时间​就是​ \( R \)。​这​有助于​评估​任务调度​器​的​效率​。

docs.title: 4. Little's Law ​的​威力​：​通用性​与​简洁性
docs.text:
Little's Law​之所以​如此​重要​，​是因为​它​的​普适性​：

  1. ​无需​指定​分布​：​它​不​要求​请求​到达​的​时间​间隔​服从​什么​分布​（​比如​泊松​分布​），​也​不​要求​处理​时间​服从​什么​分布​（​比如​指数分布​）。​只要​系统​是​稳定​的​（​即​长期​来看​，​进入​速率​等于​离开​速率​），​这个​定律​就​成立​。
  2. ​黑盒​分析​：​不​需要​知道​系统​内部​的​复杂​逻辑​，​只​需要​测量​输入​、​输出​和​内部​计数​，​就​能​推断​第三个​参数​。

docs.title: 6. ​适用​条件​与​局限性
docs.text:
​虽然​Little's Law​很​强大​，​但​它​也​有​一些​前提条件​：

  • ​稳定性​：​系统​必须​处于​稳定​状态​，​即​长期​来看​，​任务​到达​速率​等于​完成​任务​离开​的​速率​。​系统​不能​是​无限​增长​或​刚刚​启动​的​瞬态​状态​。
  • ​守恒​：​进入​系统​的​请求​最终​必须​离开​系统​（​不会​丢失​或​无限期​卡死​）。

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• ISA(Instruction Set Architecture):
    1. Interface/contract between SW and HW.
    2. What the programmer assumes hardware will satisfy
  • Microarchitecture: An implementation of the ISA
  • Digital logic circuits: Building blocks of micro-arch (e.g., gates)

docs.title: Von Neumann Model
docs.text:
• von Neumann Model consists of 5 components
    • Memory (stores the program and data)
    • Processing unit
    • Input
    • Output
    • Control unit (controls the order in which instructions are carried out)
  • Von Neumann model is also called stored program computer (instructions in memory)

Two properties:

  1. Stored program
    • Instructions stored in a linear memory array
    • Memory is unified between instructions and data
    • The interpretation of a stored value depends on the control signals
  2. Sequential instruction processing
    • One instruction processed (fetched, executed, completed) at a time
    • Program counter (instruction pointer) identifies the current instruction
    • Program counter is advanced sequentially except for control transfer instructions

docs.title: Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
docs.text:
• Intuition of instruction set
    • Instructions are words in the language of a computer
    • Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the vocabulary
  • The ISA is the interface between what the software commands and what the hardware carries out.

The ISA specifies three components:

  1. The memory organization
    • Address space (MIPS: 232)
    • Addressability (MIPS: 8 bits)
    • Word- or Byte-addressable
  2. The register set
    • 32 registers in MIPS
  3. The instruction set: cover all the tasks needed
    • Opcodes
    • Data types
    • Addressing modes

Three Main Instruction Types in MIPS:

  1. Operate instructions
    • Execute instructions in the ALU
  2. Data movement instructions
    • Read from or write to memory
  3. Control flow instructions
    • Change the sequence of execution

Complex vs. Simple Instructions:

  • Advantages of Complex instructions
    • Denser encoding -> smaller code size -> better memory utilization, saves off-chip bandwidth, better cache hit rate (better packing of instructions)
    • Simpler compiler: no need to optimize small instructions as much
  • Disadvantages of Complex Instructions
    • Larger chunks of work -> compiler has less opportunity to optimize (limited in fine-grained optimizations it can do)
    • More complex hardware -> translation from a high level to control signals and optimization needs to be done by hardware

docs.title: Instruction Processing Cycle
docs.text:
The instruction cycle is a sequence of steps or phases, that an instruction goes through to be executed

  1. Instruction fetch (IF)
  2. Instruction decode and register operand fetch (ID/RF)
  3. Execute/Evaluate memory address (EX/AG)
  4. Memory operand fetch (MEM)
  5. Store/writeback result (WB)

Not all instructions have the five phases

docs.title: Single-Cycle CPU
docs.text:
• Each instruction takes a single clock cycle to execute.
  • Only combinational logic is used to implement instruction execution
  • The slowest instruction determines the frequency

docs.title: Multi-Cycle CPU
docs.text:
Goal: Let each instruction take (close to) only as many cycles it really needs

Ideas of multi-cycle CPU:

  1. Decrease clock cycle time

  2. Each instruction takes as many clock cycles as it needs to take

    • Multiple state transitions per instruction
    • The states followed by each instruction is different

  3. FSM of Multi-Cycle CPU

docs.title: Benifits and Downsides
docs.text:
The benifits:

  1. Critical path design
    • Can keep reducing the critical path independently of the worst-case processing time of any instruction
  2. Bread and butter (common case) design
    • Can optimize the number of states it takes to execute “important” instructions that make up much of the execution time
  3. Balanced design
    • No need to provide more capability or resources than really needed
      • An instruction that needs resource X multiple times does not require multiple X’s to be implemented
      • Leads to more efficient hardware: Can reuse hardware components needed multiple times for an instruction

Downsides:

  • Need to store the intermediate results at the end of each clock cycle
    • Hardware overhead for registers
    • Register setup/hold overhead paid multiple times for an instruction
  • Limited concurrency

docs.title: Cache Coherence
docs.text:
• Cache coherence: Multiple cores have a consistent state of the last written value from any core to a memory address.

Feature:

Hardware architecture for cache coherence:

  • Cores, caches, interconnect, memory work together to achieve cache coherence from core’s point of view.
    • Cache Tags: MESI (CPU action  Bus action, Tags)
    • Cache Updating: invl./update (Bus action)
    • Interconnect: Bus/Switch

docs.title: Cache Interconnect
docs.text:
Cache Interconnect: cores communicate with each other.

  • Bus:
    • One valid at a time
    • Typically used by Snooping
  • Switch:
    • Peer-to-peer communication
    • Typically used by directory

docs.title: Bus-based Protocol
docs.text:
1. A cache arbitrates for bus access, waiting until 2 happens
  2. A cache is granted bus access
  3. A cache places command on bus, waiting until 4 happens
  4. Other caches place responses on bus

docs.title: Switch-based Protocol
docs.text: • Switch-based protocol: Each core pair can independently communicate with each other

docs.title: Cache Updating
docs.text:
Cache Updating Policy: safely update replicated data in other caches.

  • Update Protocol: Push a update command (bus action) to all copies
  • Invalidate Protocol: Ensure only one local copy by sending out an invalidation command (bus action), then update the local copy

docs.title: Bus Action: Update vs. Invalidate
docs.text:
Where and When: On a bus action write miss:

  • Update Protocol:
    • Broadcast written data and address to cores
    • Cores update the data in their caches if block is present
  • Invalidate Protocol:
    • Broadcast invalidation of address to sharers
    • Cores invalidate block in their caches if block is present

Tradeoffs:

Which do we want: Write frequency and sharing behavior are critical

  • Update Protocol
    • Advantage: If sharer set is constant and updates are infrequent, avoids the cost of invalidate-reacquire (broadcast update pattern)
    • If data is rewritten without intervening reads by other cores, updates would be useless
    • Write-through cache policy -> bus becomes bottleneck
  • Invalidate Protocol:
    • After invalidation broadcast, core has exclusive access rights
    • Only cores that keep reading after each write retain a copy
    • Disadvantage: If write contention is high, leads to ping-ponging (rapid invalidation-reacquire traffic from different processors)

Update vs. Invalidate

​特性​ Update Invalidate ​写​操作​时​的​广播​内容​ ​新​数据​值​ ​失效​信号​（​不​携带​数据​） ​其他​核心​后续​读​ ​立即​得到​最新​值​（​本地​已​更新​） ​发生​缺失​，​需拉取​新值​ ​适用​场景​ ​共享​集​固定​、​读多​写少​ ​写​操作​频繁​、​或​数据​有​写者​独占​倾向​ ​最大​风险​ ​总线​带宽​被​无用​的​更新​占​满​ ​写​竞争​激烈​时​的​乒乓​效应​ ​典型​硬件​ ​极少​用于​现代​ CPU（​如​ IBM ​某些​系统​曾用​） ​几乎​通用​（MESI ​及其​衍生​）

docs.title: MSI Protocol
docs.text:
• MSI Protocol: safely update replicated data in caches (goal).

    • I(nvalid): block is not in cache, need to fetch from memory or other cache
    • S(hared): in >=1 caches, clean, local cores can read it w/o bus action
    • M(odified): in 1 cache, core can read/write it w/o bus action

  • State Diagram for CPU Requests:

  • State Diagrams for Bus Requests:

The Problem with MSI:

  • A block is not in cache at the beginning. On a read, the block immediately goes to the “Shared” state.
  • Problem: The core issues a bus action invalidate before writing the block to cache, even when only one cache copy exists.

docs.title: MESI Protocol
docs.text:
• MESI Protocol: Illinois protocol (ISCA, 84)
    • I(nvalid): block is not in cache, need to fetch from memory or other cache
    • S(hared): in >1 caches, clean, local cores directly reads it w/o bus action
    • M(odified): in 1 cache, local core can read/write it w/o bus action
    • E(xclusive): in 1 cache, clean, local core reads/writes it w/o bus action

Key Differences from MSI Protocol:

  • Local core reads block in state E, the state holds
  • Local core writes block in state E -> state M, without bus action
  • Remote core reads, via read miss on bus, block in state E -> state S
  • Remote core writes, via write miss on bus, block in state E -> state I

docs.title: Cache Snoop Protocol
docs.text:
Snoop: [Goodman ISCA 1983]

  • Single point of serialization for all memory requests
  • One outstanding memory request per processor
  • System interconnect is an atomic shared bus (one cache communicates at a time)

How Snoop/Direct works

- Initial states: X is only shared by C3 and C4 - Operations: - C1:X=888 - C3: reads X - C1: X=888 - C3: reads X

Why needing a Bus?

  • Ordering
    • Bus serializes requests, ordering some before others.
    • However: coherence does not require ordering of requests to different address.
  • Communication
    • Simple, fast broadcast medium
    • However: coherence does not require broadcast
      • Only need to communicate with sharers
      • Observation: most data is not shared by every cache.

docs.title: Directory-Based Cache Coherence
docs.text:
• Goal: address the lack of scalability of snooping protocols.
    • All-to-all broadcast will not scale
  • Idea: A logically-central directory keeps track of where the copies of each cache block reside. Caches consult this directory to ensure coherence.
    • Coherence still requires single point of serialization (for write serialization)
    • Serialization location can be different for every block (striped across nodes/memory-controllers)

docs.title: Directory: Node Definition
docs.text:
Regarding a cache block:

  • Home Node: the node owns the corresponding directory, each cache block can have different home node
  • Local Node: the node initiates the cache read/write requests
  • Remote Node: the node passively responses to the action from the home node

docs.title: Directory: Basic Operations
docs.text:
Local node:

  • On a bus read: send out getS request to directory node, after receiving the data, set the cache’s bit.
  • On a bus write: send out getEx request to directory node
    • invalidate all caches that have the block and reset their bits
    • Have an “exclusive bit” associated with each block in each cache

Directory node:

  1. Receives getS, getEx requests from nodes
  2. Based on different cache states:
    1. Sends Invalidate messages to sharers if needed
    2. Forwards request to memory if needed
  3. Replies to requestor and updates sharing state

Detailed directory for each cache line

Each cache block needs N+log2N + 2 bits for its directory, which resides at the home node.

  • 2-bit cache states: a block is owned by the directory unless the block is in a cache in state M. State M means a node writes to it.
  • One shared bit for each cache: indicating whether the block is shared in a cache
  • log2N owner bit: indicates that the cache that has the only copy of the block and can update it without notifying others

How Directory works

  • Initial states:
    • Directory stays in C2
    • X is only shared by C3 and C4

  • Operations:

    • C1:X=888
    • C3: reads X

  • C1:X=888

  • C3: reads X

docs.title: Ordering of operations
docs.text:
Operations: A, B, C, D

In what order should the hardware execute (and report the results of) these operations?

Consistency： A contract between programmer and microarchitect.

  • Preserving an “expected” (more accurately, “agreed upon”) order simplifies programmer’s life
    • Ease of debugging; ease of state recovery, exception handling
  • Preserving an “expected” order usually makes the hardware designer’s life difficult
    • Especially if the goal is to design a high performance processor: Recall load-store queues in out of order execution and their complexity

docs.title: Memory Ordering in a single processor
docs.text:
Specified by the von Neumann model

  • Sequential order: Hardware executes the load and store operations in the order specified by the sequential program

  • Out-of-order execution does not change the semantics

    • Hardware retires (reports to software the results of) the load and store operations in the order specified by the sequential program

Advantages:

1) Architectural state is precise within an execution. 2) Architectural state is consistent across different runs of the program -> Easier to debug programs

Disadvantage:

  • Preserving order adds overhead, reduces performance, increases complexity, reduces scalability

docs.title: Memory Ordering in a MIMD Processor
docs.text:
Each processor’s memory operations are in sequential order with respect to the “thread” running on that processor (assume each processor obeys the von Neumann model)

Multiple processors execute memory operations concurrently

  • How does the memory see the order of operations from all processors?
  • In other words, what is the ordering of operations across different processors?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Is it possible for both cores to enter critical section and to print “Hello” and “ZJU” on real hardware?

  • Challenge: The two processors did NOT see the same order of operations to memory
  • The “happened before” relationship between multiple updates to memory was inconsistent between the two processors’ points of view
  • As a result, each processor thought the other was not in the critical section

Memory Barrier

​内存​屏障​用于​强制​禁止​特定​顺序​的​重排​。

Consistency Model:

Load-Load Load-Store Store-Store Store-Load Consistency Model CPU ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Sequential Consistency Dual 386 ✓ ✓ ✓ Total Store Order X86/64 ✓ ✓ Partial Store Order Arm Really weak memory model DEC Alpha
  • The stronger memory model leads to lower performance/higher overhead
  • The stronger memory model makes programmers’ life easier

docs.title: 1. Load-Load Barrier
docs.text:
• ​定义​：​禁止​屏障​之前​的​读​操作​与​屏障​之后​的​读​操作​重排​。
  • ​效果​：​保证​所有​在​屏障​前​的​ LOAD ​都​完成​后​，​才能​执行​屏障​后​的​ LOAD。
  • ​伪​代码​： 
    LOAD A
LOAD-LOAD barrier
LOAD B   // ​保证​在​ LOAD A ​之后​执行​
  • ​典型​用途​：​用于​确保​先​读取​某个​标志​，​再​读取​由该​标志​保护​的​数据​（​类似​于​ READ_ONCE + ​屏障​顺序​）。

docs.title: 2. Load-Store Barrier
docs.text:
• ​定义​：​禁止​屏障​之前​的​读​操作​与​屏障​之后​的​写​操作​重排​。
  • ​效果​：​屏障​前​的​所有​ LOAD ​必须​在​屏障​后​的​ STORE ​之前​完成​。
  • ​伪​代码​： 
    LOAD A
LOAD-STORE barrier
STORE B   // ​保证​在​ LOAD A ​之后​才能​写​ B
  • ​典型​用途​：​常见于​获取​锁​（lock acquire）：​先​读取​锁​变量​的​值​（​判断​是否​可用​），​然后​写入​新值​（​持有​锁​）。​屏障​保证​读取​锁​状态​完成​后​才​进行​写入​。

docs.title: 3. Store-Store Barrier
docs.text:
• ​定义​：​禁止​屏障​之前​的​写​操作​与​屏障​之后​的​写​操作​重排​。
  • ​效果​：​屏障​前​的​所有​ STORE ​对​内存​可见​后​，​才能​执行​屏障​后​的​ STORE。
  • ​伪​代码​： 
    STORE A
STORE-STORE barrier
STORE B   // ​保证​在​ STORE A ​对​其他​核心​可见​后​，​才​执行​ STORE B
  • ​典型​用途​：​用于​释放​锁​（lock release）：​先​更新​共享​数据​，​再​更新​锁​变量​（​表示​无锁​）。​屏障​保证数据​写​操作​在​锁​状态​写​操作​之前​全局​可见​。

docs.title: 4. Store-Load Barrier
docs.text:
• ​定义​：​禁止​屏障​之前​的​写​操作​与​屏障​之后​的​读​操作​重排​。
  • ​效果​：​屏障​前​的​所有​ STORE ​必须​全局​可见​后​，​才能​执行​屏障​后​的​ LOAD。
  • ​伪​代码​： 
    STORE A
STORE-LOAD barrier
LOAD B    // ​保证​在​ STORE A ​对​其他​核心​可见​后​，​才​读取​ B
  • ​特性​：​这​是​最​昂贵​的​屏障​，​因为​它​要求​写​缓冲​（store buffer）​完全​清空​并​刷新​到​缓存​/​内存​，​才能​读取​新值​。x86 ​的​ mfence ​提供​这种​屏障​
  • ​典型​用途​：​实现​顺序​一致性​的​跨​线程​同步​，​例如​无锁​算法​中​的​发布​-​订阅​模式​：​线程​ 1 ​写​数据​，​写​标志​；​线程​ 2 ​读​标志​，​读数据​。​若​线程​ 2 ​先读​到​新​标志​但读​到​的​数据​是​旧​的​（​因​重排​），​则​会​出错​。Store-Load ​屏障​可​阻止​这种​“​写后​读​”​的​重排​。

docs.title: Sequential Consistency
docs.text:
Load-Load Load-Store Store-Store Store-Load

Sequential Consistency in a multiprocessor system if:

  • In uniprocessor: the operations of each individual processor appear in this sequence in the order specified by its program AND
  • In multiprocessor: the result of any execution is the same as if the operations of all the processors were executed in some sequential order, as if they were manipulating a single shared memory

Sequential Consistency: Memory is a switch that serves one load or store at a time from any processor

  • All processors see the currently serviced load or store at the same time
  • Each processor’s operations are serviced in program order
  • Problem of Sequential Consistency: low performance
    • Two instructions do not conflict, but the second instruction still needs have to wait for the first one to finish before executing.
    • Writing to memory is really slow, e.g., 100 cycles

  • Reasonable execution order:
  • 1->2->3->4 "Hello"
  • 3->4->1->2 "ZJU"
  • 1->3->2->4 or 1->3->4->2
  • 3->1->2->4 or 3->1->4->2

docs.title: Total Store Order
docs.text:
Load-Load Load-Store Store-Store

Total Store Order == SC + Store buffer:

  • SC: Sequential Consistency
  • Committing a store instruction means the data is stored in store buffer, rather than cache hierarchy.
  • The store instruction writes in a local store buffer and then proceed to next instruction (e.g., load) immediately.
  • The cache will pull writes out of the store buffer when ready.
  • Store-load order is not preserved.

Idea of store buffer：

  • Overlap memory accesses with other accesses and computation.
  • Hide long write latency in the core
  • Reordering read before store

  • Is it possible to print “Hello” and “ZJU” on real hardware?
    • under total store order: 2->4->1->3 or 2->4->3->1

docs.title: Partial Store Order
docs.text:
• Load-Load
  • Load-Store

Partial Store Order == Total Store Order + Write coalescing：

  • Write coalescing: merge writes to the same cache line inside the write buffer to save memory bandwidth
  • Store-store order is not preserved.

Intuitive Example of Write Coalescing：

docs.title: Why Cache Consistency Even Matter?
docs.text:
• Ease of debugging
    • It is nice to have the same execution done at different times to have the same order of execution -> Repeatability
  • Correctness
    • Can we have incorrect execution if the order of memory operations is different from the point of view of different processors?
  • Performance and overhead
    • Enforcing a strict “sequential ordering” can make life harder for the hardware designer in implementing performance enhancement techniques (e.g., OoO execution, caches)

docs.title: Protecting Shared Data
docs.text:
When Could Order Affect Correctness: When protecting shared data

  • Threads are not allowed to update shared data concurrently
    • For correctness purposes
  • Accesses to shared data are encapsulated inside critical sections or protected via synchronization constructs (locks, semaphores, condition variables)
  • Mutual exclusion principle: Only one thread can execute a critical section at a given time.
  • A multiprocessor should provide the correct execution of synchronization primitives to enable the programmer to protect shared data

docs.title: Supporting Mutual Exclusion
docs.text:
• Programmer relies on hardware primitives to support correct synchronization
    • If hardware primitives are not correct (or unpredictable), programmer’s life is tough
    • If hardware primitives are correct but not easy to reason about or use, programmer’s life is still tough
  • Programmer needs to make sure mutual exclusion (synchronization) is correctly implemented
    • But, correct parallel programming is an important topic
    • Coherence is cheaper than OS-level barrier

docs.title: Memory Model in GPU Architecture
docs.text:
• Cache Consistency Issue:
    • Each SM writes data to its L1 cache, which does not affect shared L2 cache immediately.
    • Manually use PTX instructions to write data to L2 or global memory

docs.title: Multi-level Caching in a pipelined design
docs.text:
First-level caches (instruction and data):

  • Decisions very much affected by cycle time
  • Small, lower associativity; latency is critical
  • Tag store and data store usually accessed in parallel

Second-level caches:

  • Decisions need to balance hit rate and access latency
  • Usually large and highly associative; latency not as important
  • Tag store and data store can be accessed serially

Serial vs. Parallel access of levels:

  • Serial: Second level cache accessed only if first-level misses
  • Second level does not see the same accesses as the first
    • First level acts as a filter (filters some temporal and spatial locality)
    • Management policies are therefore different

docs.title: Why cache
docs.text:
Problem of idea memory:

  • Bigger is slower
  • Faster is more expensive
  • Higher bandwidth is more expensive

CPU wants both fast (~1ns) and large memory (GB) without modifying user code. But we cannot achieve both with a single level of memory

  • Idea:

    • Have multiple levels of storage (progressively bigger and slower as the levels are farther from the processor) and
    • Ensure most of the data the processor needed is kept in the fast(er) level(s).

  • New Memory Hierarchy

docs.title: Why cache works: locality
docs.text:
• Locality: One’s recent past is a very good predictor of his/her near future.

  • Temporal Locality: A program tends to reference the same memory location many times and all within a small window of time

  • Spatial Locality: A program tends to reference nearby memory locations within a window of time
    • most notable examples:
      1. instruction memory references -> most sequential/streaming
      2. references to arrays/vectors -> often streaming/strided

docs.title: Exploit temporal locality
docs.text:
• Idea: Store recently accessed data in automatically managed fast memory(cache)
  • Anticipation: same mem. location will be accessed again soon
  • Temporal locality principle:
    • Recently accessed data will be again accessed in the near future

docs.title: Exploit spatial locality
docs.text:
• Idea: Store data in addresses adjacent to the recently accessed one in automatically-managed fast memory
    • logically divide memory into equal-size blocks
    • Fetch to cache the accessed block in its entirely
  • Anticipation: nearby memory location will be accessed soon
  • Temporal locality principle:
    • Nearby data in memory will be accessed in the near future

docs.title: Cache hierarchy
docs.text:
• The cache needs to be tightly integrated into the pipeline
    • Ideally, access in 1-cycle so that load-dependent operations do not stall
  • High frequency pipeline -> Cannot make the cache large(to ensure access in 1-cycle)

But, we want a large cache AND a pipelined design

  • Idea: Cache hierarchy

docs.title: Hierarchical latency analysis
docs.text:
• For a given memory hierarchy level i it has a technology-intrinsic access time of \(t_i\), The perceived access time \(T_i\) is longer than \(t_i\)
  • Except for the outer-most hierarchy, when looking for a given address there is
    • a chance (hit-rate \(hr_i\)) you “hit” and access time is \(t_i\)
    • a chance (miss-rate \(mr_i\)) you “miss” and access time \(t_i + T_{i+1}\)
    • \(hr_i + mr_i =1\)
  • Thus, \(T_i=hr_i*t_i + mr_i*(t_i+T_{i+1})\) \(T_i = t_i + mr_i*T_{i+1}\)
  • Our goal: achieve desired \(T_i\) within allowed cost
  • \(T_i \approx t_i\) is desirable when
    • keep \(mr_i\) low:
      1. increasing capacity \(C_i\), but beware of increasing \(t_i\)
      2. use smarter cache management(anticipate what is needed and not needed)
    • keep \(T_{i+1}\) low
      1. faster lower hierarchies, but beware of increasing cost
      2. introduce intermediate hierarchies as a compromise

docs.title: What is cache
docs.text:
• Any structure that “memorizes” frequently used results/data
    • to avoid repeating the long-latency operations required to reproduce/fetch the results/data from scratch
    • e.g., a web cache
  • Most commonly in the processor design context: an automatically-managed memory structure
    • e.g., memorize in fast SRAM the most frequently or recently accessed DRAM memory locations to avoid repeatedly paying for the DRAM access latency

docs.title: Cache Metrics
docs.text:
• Average memory access time(AMAT):
    • AMAT=(hit-rate * hit-latency) + (miss-rate * miss-latency)

docs.title: Addressing the Cache
docs.text:
Cache access:

1) index into the tag and data stores with index bits in address; 2) checks valid bit in tag store; 3) compares tag bits in address with the stored tag in tag store; 4) If a block is in the cache (cache hit), the stored tag should be valid and match the tag of the block, and read out data.

docs.title: Cache Basics
docs.text:
• Cache Block (line): Unit of storage in the cache

    • Memory is logically divided into blocks that map to potential locations in the cache.

  • On a reference:

    • HIT: If in cache, use cached data instead of accessing memory
    • MISS: If not in cache, bring block into cache
      • May have to evict some other block

  • For high cache hit rate, important cache design decisions:

    • Placement: where and how to place/find a block in cache?
    • Replacement: what data to remove to make room in cache?
    • Granularity of management: large or small blocks? Subblocks?
    • Write policy: what do we do about writes?
    • Instructions/data: do we treat them separately?

docs.title: Cache: Placement
docs.text:
• A key question: How to map chunks of the main memory address space to blocks in the cache?

Three Cache Organization Methods:

  • Fully-associative: A chunk can go to any cache block in the cache
  • Direct mapped: A chunk can go to only one cache block in the cache
  • Set-associative: A chunk can go to N cache blocks in the N-way set-associative cache

docs.title: Direc-Mapped Cache: Placement and Access
docs.text:
• Two blocks in memory that map to the same index in the cache cannot be present in the cache at the same time
    • one index -> one entry
  • Main advantage: easy to implement
  • Main issue: Can lead to 0% hit rate if more than one block accessed in an interleaved manner map to the same index
    • Asumme addresses A and B have the same index bits but different interleaved manner map to the same index
    • A,B,A,B,A,B,...->conflict in the cache index
    • All accesses are conflict misses

docs.title: Full Associativity
docs.text:
• Advantage: high utilization of cache blocks
  • Issue: can lead to extremely difficult to implement when the number of cache blocks in the cache is large
    • Number of cache blocks in modern CPU reaches 32M/64=512K.
    • Choosing one out of 512K cache lines is extremely costly.

docs.title: Set-Associative Cache
docs.text:
• 2-way cache: have 2 columns of 4 blocks
  • 4-way Set Associativity
  • Advantages: accommodates conflicts better(fewer conflict misses)
    • Assume addresses A and B have the same index bits but different tag bits
    • A, B, A, B, A, B, A, B, … -> store in the cache set
    • All accesses are cache hit
  • Issue of Set-associative cache
    • more complex, slower access, larger tag store

docs.title: Associativity and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Degree of associativity: how many blocks can map to the same index(or set)?
  • Higher associativity:
    • higher hit rate
    • slower cache access time(hit latency and data access latency)
    • more expensive hardware(more components)
  • Diminishing returns from higher associativity

docs.title: Cache: Replacement
docs.text:
• Replacement in set-associative caches

  • Key challenge: which cache block in a set be replaced once new block comes?

  • Any invalid block first

  • If all are valid, consult the replacement policy:
    • Random
    • FIFO
    • Least recently used(LRU)
    • Hybrid replacement policies
    • Optimal replacement policy?

docs.title: Implementing LRU
docs.text:
• Idea: Evict the least recently accessed block
  • Problem: need to keep track of access ordering of blocks(challeging in hardware)
  • Approximatoins of LRU:

Pseudo LRU for 8-way set-associated cache

  • Assume 8 blocks (L0~L7) for a set, 7 rule bits (B0~B6).

  • PLRU Replacement Way Selection: choosing the suitable way (L0~L7) based on the PLRU bits.

  • PLRU Bits Updating Rule: updating PLRU bits after replacing the way (L0~L7).

LRU or Random

  • LRU is not always better than random:
    • Example: 4-way cache, cyclic references to A, B, C, D, E
  • Set thrashing: When the "program working set" in a set is larger than set associativity
    • Random replacement policy is better when thrashing occurs(example above)
  • Which one is better in practice?
    • depends on workload
    • average hit rate of LRU and Random are similar
  • Best of both worlds: hybrid of LRU and Random
    • intel CPU uses the hybrid approach

docs.title: Optimal policy
docs.text:
Belady’s OPT (Optimal Replacement)

  • replace the block that is going to be referenced furthest in the future by the program
  • No possibility to implement in theory

docs.title: Cache: Write policy
docs.text:
Where should you write the result of a store? One policy for each step.

  • Step1: store ins -> cache(write miss), either policy works

    • write-allocate(memory, default):
      • allocate the cache line(put it in the cache)
      • issue: read an entire cache block from memory
    • write-no-allocate policy(PCIe/IO):
      • write in directly to memory without allocation in cache
      • ignore cache

  • Step2: cache -> memory(write hit), either policy works:

    • write-back policy(default):
      • writes it to the cache and wait until the cache kicks the cache block out
    • write-through policy(streaming write instruction):
      • writes it to the cache and memory right away

write-back vs. write-through

Write-back:

  • Write goes to cache; cache writes to main memory (evicted)
  • Can combine multiple writes to the same block before eviction
    • potentially saves bandwidth between cache levels and saves energy
  • But need a bit in the tag store indicating the block is "dirty/modified"

Write-through:

  • Write goes to memory and cache
  • Simpler, evictions do not need to write to memory
  • All levels are up to date: consistency——simpler cache coherence because no need to check close-to-processor caches' tag stores for presence
  • But more memory bandwidth intensive; no combining of writes

docs.title: Instruction vs. Data Caches
docs.text:
Core question: separate of unified

Pros and cons of unified cache:

  • Pros: Dynamic sharing of cache space: no overprovisioning that might happen with static partitioning (i.e., separate I and D caches)
  • Instructions and data can thrash each other (i.e., no guaranteed space for either)
  • I and D are accessed in different places in the pipeline. Where do we place the unified cache for fast access?

Modern CPU:

  • First level caches are almost always split
  • Higher level caches are almost always unified

docs.title: Compulsory miss
docs.text:
• Defined as the first reference to an address (block), always resulting in a miss

How to reduce:

  • cache cannot help
  • prefetching can help:anticipate which block will be need soon

docs.title: Capacity miss
docs.text:
• defined as the misses that would occur even in a fully-associative cache (with optimal replacement) of the same capacity
  • Cause: cache is too small to hold everything needed

How to reduce:

  • Utilize cache space better: keep blocks that will be referenced
  • Software management: divide working set and computation such that each “computation phase” fits in cache

docs.title: Conflict miss
docs.text:
• defined as any miss that is neither a compulsory nor a capacity miss

How to reduce:

  • More associativity
  • Other ways to get more associativity without making the cache associative
    • Victim cache
    • Better, randomized indexing
    • Software hints?

docs.title: Cache performance
docs.text:
Three fundamental goals:

  • Reducing miss rate
    • Caveat: reducing miss rate can reduce performance if more costly-to-refetch blocks are evicted
  • Reducing miss latency or miss cost
  • Reducing hit latency or hit cost

Cache Terminology

  • Capacity(C): the number of data bytes a cache stores
  • Block size(b): bytes of data brought into cache at once
  • Number of blocks(B=C/b): number of blocks in cache
  • Degree of associativity(N): number of blocks in a set
  • Number of sets(S=B/N): each memory address maps to exactly one cache set

docs.title: Cache Size
docs.text:
Cache size: total data (not including tag) capacity

  • Bigger can exploit temporal locality better but not always better
  • Too large a cache adversely affects hit and miss latency
    • smaller is faster => bigger is slower
    • access time may degrade critical path
  • Too small a cache
    • doesn’t exploit temporal locality well
    • useful data replaced often

  • Working set: the whole set of data the executing application references
    • Within a time interval

docs.title: Block Size
docs.text:
• Block size is the data that is associated with an address tag
  • Too small blocks
    • don't exploit spatial locality well
    • have larger tag overhead
  • Too large blocks
    • too few total # of blocks -> less temporal locality exploitation
    • waste of cache space and bandwidth/energy if spatial locality is not high

docs.title: Associativity
docs.text:
• How many blocks can be present in the same index(i.e.,set)

  • Large associativity

    • lower miss rate(reduced conflicts)
    • higher hit latency and area cost(plus diminishing results)
  • Smaller associativity
    • lower hit rate
    • lower cost
    • lower hit latency(especially important for L1 cache)

docs.title: Cache in a multi-core CPU
docs.text:
• Cores want a consistent view of memory
  • Cache in a multi-core system

How to design cache for multiple cores?

docs.title: Private vs. Shared caches
docs.text:
• Private cache: cache belongs to one core(a shared block can be in multiple caches)
  • Shared cache: Cache is shared by multiple cores

docs.title: Resource sharing
docs.text:
• Idea: Instead of dedicating a hardware resource to a hardware context, allow multiple contexts to use it
  • Example resources: functional units, pipeline, caches, buses, memory

Advantages:

  • Resource sharing improves utilization/efficiency  throughput
    • When a resource is left idle by one thread, another thread can use it; no need to replicate shared data
  • Reduces communication latency
    • For example, data shared between multiple threads can be kept in the same cache in multithreaded processors
  • Compatible with the shared memory programming model

Disadvantages:

  • Resource sharing results in contention for resources
    • When the resource is not idle, another thread cannot use it
    • If space is occupied by one thread, another thread needs to re-occupy it
  • Sometimes reduces each or some thread’s performance
    • Thread performance can be worse than when it is run alone
  • Eliminates performance isolation -> inconsistent performance across runs
    • Thread performance depends on co-executing threads
    • Uncontrolled (free-for-all) sharing degrades QoS
    • Causes unfairness, starvation

Need to efficiently and fairly utilize shared resources

docs.title: Shared caches betweent cores
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • High effective capacity
  • Dynamic partitioning of available cache space
    • No fragmentation due to static partitioning
    • If one core does not utilize some space, another core can
  • Easier to maintain coherence (a cache block is in a single location)

Disadvantages:

  • Slower access (cache not tightly coupled with the core)
  • Cores incur conflict misses due to other cores’ accesses
    • Misses due to inter-core interference
    • Some cores can destroy the hit rate of other cores
  • Guaranteeing a minimum level of service (or fairness) to each core is harder (how much space, how much bandwidth?)

docs.title: Preserve coherence and consistence
docs.text:
Cache coherence and Memory consistency:

  • Coherence is about ordering of operations from different processors to the same memory location
    • local ordering of accesses to each cache block
  • Consistency is about ordering off all memory operations from different processors(i.e. to different memory locations)
    • global ordering of accesses to all memory locations

docs.title: 深度​学习​加速器​设计
docs.text:
• DSA：Domain Specific Architecture

5​个​DSA​设计​思想​：

  • Global Buffer: ​使用​专有​的​存储器​来​减少​数据​搬运​的​距离​与​开销​，​比如​将​复杂​的​cache​设计​替换成​scratchpad memory (global buffer)
  • ​简化​控制​模块​: ​将​缩减​的​高级​微​架构​特性​而​节省​出​的​面积​，​用于​增加​更​多​的​运算​单元​或者​片上​存储​。
  • ​并行计算​模块​: ​使用​能够​符合​特定​领域​加速​需求​最​简单​的​并行​形式​，​例如​，​对于​矩阵​运算​的​加速​，​单条​指令​直接​支持​小​矩阵​运算​。
  • ​量化​: ​减少​计算​数据​尺寸​与​类型​来​符合​特定​领域​性能​要求​，​例如​，​深度​学习​中​，​推理​可以​采用​int8​量化​方式​进行​。
  • ​专用​编程语言​: ​使用​DSA​专用​语言​进行​编程​。

CPU​冯诺​依曼​架构​简介​

​冯​.​诺​依曼结构​的​五大​基本​组件​：

  • ​输入​设备​: ​输入​数据​和​程序​
  • ​存储器​: ​记忆​程序​和​数据​
  • ​运算器​: ​完成​数据​加工​处理​
  • ​控制器​: ​控制程序​执行​

  • ​输出设备​: ​输出​处理结果​

  • CPU​支持​的​功能​：

  • CPU​很多​资源​用​在​辅助​功能​: Cache、​分支​预测​、​预取​、​中断​、​权限​等​

docs.text:

docs.text:

AI Processor​的​Superscalar：

Variable declaration Memory Scope Lifetime int LocalVar; register thread thread int localArr[N]; global thread thread __device__ __shared__ int SharedVar; shared block block __device__ int GlobalVar; global grid application __device__ __constant__ int ConstantVar; constant grid application

docs.title: Multithreading
docs.text:
• Latency Hiding via Warp-Level FGMT(Fine-grained multithreading,​细粒度​多线程​)
  • FGMT can hide long latency operations (e.g., memory accesses)
  • Occupancy: ratio of active warps to the maximum number of warps per GPU core

docs.title: Memory Coalescing
docs.text:
• Memory Coalescing:
    • When threads in the same warp access consecutive memory locations in the same burst, the accesses can be combined and served by one burst
  • Memory Divergence：
    • If threads in the same warp access locations not in the same burst, accesses cannot be combined
    • Multiple memory transactions are needed
    • Takes longer to service data to the warp

When accessing global memory, memory coalescing makes sure that concurrent threads access nearby memory locations Peak bandwidth utilization occurs when all threads in a warp access one cache line (or several consecutive cache lines)

  • Uncoalesced Memory Access

  • Coalesced Memory Access

docs.title: Shared Memory
docs.text:
• Shared memory is an interleaved (banked) memory
    • Each bank can service one address per cycle
  • Typically, 32 banks in NVIDIA GPUs
    • Successive 32-bit words are assigned to successive banks
      • Bank = Address % 32
  • Bank conflicts are only possible within a warp
    • No bank conflicts between different warps

docs.text:
• Bank conflict tree

docs.text:
• No data reuse: each thread reads its only elements

    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++){
        sum += gauss[i][j] * Image[(i+row-1)*width + (j+col-1)];

  • Data reuse: divide the input into tiles, each of which loads L_SIZE chunks together into shared memory, then compute together

…
Load tile into shared memory l_data

for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++){

synchronization function
  • void __synchronizes(): synchronize all threads in a block
  • Once all threads in a block have reached this point, execution resumes normally
  • Used to avoid RAW / WAR / WAW hazards when accessing shared or global memory

docs.title: Tiling/Blocking in On-chip memories
docs.text:
Tiling or Blocking

  • Divide loops operating on arrays into computation chunks so that each chunk can hold its data in the on-chip RAM (or other on-chip memory, e.g., scratchpad)

  • Avoids on-chip RAM conflicts between different chunks of computation

  • Essentially: Divide the working set so that each piece fits in the on-chip RAMs

docs.title: CPU: Tiled Matrix Multiplication
docs.text:
• Tiled Matrix Multiplication: Achieve better on-chip RAM locality by computing on smaller tiles or blocks that fit in the RAMs

  • Tiled implementation operates on submatrices (tiles or blocks) that fit fast RAMs (cache, scratchpad, RF)

docs.title: GPU: Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
docs.text:
• Parallelization approach: assign one thread to each element in the output matrix (C)
__global__ void mm_kernel(float* A, float* B, float* C, unsigned int N) {

    unsigned int row = blockIdx.y*blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    unsigned int col = blockIdx.x*blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

    float sum = 0.0f;
    for(unsigned int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        sum += A[row*N + i]*B[i*N + col];
    }
    C[row*N + col] = sum;

}

docs.title: GPU: Tiled Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
docs.text:
• Insight: Some of the threads in the same thread block use the same input data

  • Step 1: Load the first tile of each input matrix to shared memory (each thread loads one element)

  • Step 2: Each thread computes its partial sum from the tiles in shared memory (threads wait for each other to finish)

Code
  • Host:
int N = 1024; // ​假设​矩阵​为​ 1024x1024
size_t bytes = N * N * sizeof(float);

// ​分配​显存​
float *d_A, *d_B, *d_C;
cudaMalloc(&d_A, bytes);
cudaMalloc(&d_B, bytes);
cudaMalloc(&d_C, bytes);

// ​拷贝​数据​到​显存​（​略​）

// ​配置​内核​启动​参数​
dim3 threads(TILE_SIZE, TILE_SIZE); // 16x16 = 256 ​线程​/Block
dim3 blocks((N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE, 
            (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE);

// ​启动​核​函数​
matrixMulShared<<<blocks, threads>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, N);

// ​注意​：​记得​用​ cudaDeviceSynchronize(); ​和​ cudaGetLastError(); ​检查​错误​
  • Device:
// ​定义​分块​大小​，​通常​设​为​ 16 ​或​ 32（​针对​现代​ GPU ​的​ 32 ​线程​ Warp ​优化​）
#define TILE_SIZE 16

__global__ void matrixMulShared(float *A, float *B, float *C, int N) {
    // 1. ​确定​当前​线程​在​网格​中​的​全局​位置​
    int row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.x;

    // 2. ​声明​共享内存​（__shared__），​生命周期​为​整个​ Block
    //    ​每个​ Block ​拥有​自己​的​ TILE_SIZE * TILE_SIZE ​小​块​数据​
    __shared__ float subA[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
    __shared__ float subB[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];

    float sum = 0.0f; // ​用​寄存器​存​局部​累加​和​，​极大​减少​对​ C ​数组​的​读写​

    // 3. ​遍历​所有​分块​（​将​ A ​按列​分块​，B ​按行​分块​）
    //    k_start ​是​ A ​的​列​偏移​，​也​是​ B ​的​行​偏移​
    for (int k_start = 0; k_start < N; k_start += TILE_SIZE) {

        // --- ​阶段​一​：​协同​加载​（Coalesced Load）--- 
        // ​将​全局​内存​中​的​数据​加载​到​共享内存​
        // ​条件​判断​是​为了​处理​ N ​不能​被​ TILE_SIZE ​整除​的​边界​情况​
        if (row < N && (k_start + threadIdx.x) < N) {
            subA[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = A[row * N + (k_start + threadIdx.x)];
        } else {
            subA[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f; // ​越界​补​ 0
        }

        if ((k_start + threadIdx.y) < N && col < N) {
            subB[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = B[(k_start + threadIdx.y) * N + col];
        } else {
            subB[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f;
        }

        // ​同步​：​确保​整个​ Block ​的​所有​线程​都​把​数据​搬进​ Shared Memory ​后​，​再​开始​计算​
        __syncthreads();

        // --- ​阶段​二​：​计算​（Compute）---
        // ​此时​数据​已经​在​ L1 ​缓存​级别​的​共享内存​中​，​访问速度​极快​（​约​ 1.5 TB/s）
        for (int k = 0; k < TILE_SIZE; k++) {
            sum += subA[threadIdx.y][k] * subB[k][threadIdx.x];
        }

        // ​同步​：​确保​所有​线程​都​算​完​这​一轮​，​再​进入​下​一轮​循环​覆盖​共享内存​中​的​数据​
        __syncthreads();
    }

    // 4. ​将​最终​结果​写回​全局​内存​
    if (row < N && col < N) {
        C[row * N + col] = sum;
    }
}

docs.title: Divergency
docs.text:
• A GPU uses a SIMT pipeline to save area on control logic: Groups scalar threads into warps

  • Branch divergence occurs when threads inside warps branch to different execution paths

docs.title: SIMT Utilization
docs.text:
• Intra-warp divergence
Compute(threadIdx.x);
if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0){
  Do_this(threadIdx.x);
}
else{
  Do_that(threadIdx.x);
}
  • Divergence-free execution:
Compute(threadIdx.x);
if (threadIdx.x < 32){
  Do_this(threadIdx.x * 2);
}
else{
  Do_that((threadIdx.x%32)*2+1);
}

docs.title: Vector reduction
docs.text:
• Program with low SIMD utilization:

    __shared__ float partialSum[]

unsigned int t = threadIdx.x;

for (int stride = 1; stride < blockDim.x; stride *= 2) {

__syncthreads();

if (t % (2*stride) == 0)
    partialSum[t] += partialSum[t + stride];
}

Divergence-Free Mapping:

  • All active threads belong to the same warp

  • Program with high SIMD utilization:

unsigned int t = threadIdx.x;

for (int stride = blockDim.x; stride > 0;  stride >> 1){

__syncthreads();

if (t < stride)
    partialSum[t] += partialSum[t + stride];
}

docs.title: Atomic Operations
docs.text:
• Use atomic operations to prevent data races when more than one thread need to update the same memory location

  • Atomic operations serialize the execution if there are atomic conflicts:

  • Computation

    • Atomics on an array that will be the output of the kernel
    • Example: Histogram, reduction

  • Synchronization

    • Atomics on memory locations that are used for synchronization or coordination
    • Example: Counters, locks, flags…

docs.title: CPU-GPU Transfer
docs.text:
CUDA streams (command queues in OpenCL)

Sequence of operations that are performed in order

  1. Data transfer CPU-GPU
  2. Kernel execution
    • D input data instances, B blocks
  3. Data transfer GPU-CPU

Estimates

  • \(t_E >= t_T\)(dominant kernel): \(t_E + \frac{t_T}{\#Streams}\)
  • \(t_T >= t_E\)(dominant transfer): \(t_T + \frac{t_E}{\#Streams}\)
Example code 
// Create streams
int number_of_streams = 32;
cudaStream_t stream[number_of_streams]; // Stream declaration
for(int i = 0; i < number_of_streams; ++i)
    cudaStreamCreate(&stream[i]); // Stream creation


// CPU-GPU data transfers
for (int i = 0; i < number_of_streams; ++i)
    cudaMemcpyAsync(inputDevPtr + i * size, hostPtr + i * size, size, 
                    cudaMemcpyHostToDevice, stream[i]);

// Kernel launches
for (int i = 0; i < number_of_streams; ++i)
    MyKernel<<<num_blocks / number_of_streams, num_threads, 0, stream[i]>>>
                            (outputDevPtr + i * size, inputDevPtr + i * size, size);

// GPU-CPU data transfers
for (int i = 0; i < number_of_streams; ++i)
    cudaMemcpyAsync(hostPtr + i * size, outputDevPtr + i * size, size, 
                    cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost, stream[i]);

cudaDeviceSynchronize(); // Explicit synchronization

// Destroy streams
for (int i = 0; i < number_of_streams; ++i)
    cudaStreamDestroy(stream[i]); // Stream destruction
  • Applications with independent computation on different data instances can benefit from asynchronous transfers
  • Use case: video processing

docs.text:
• GPU Computing: computation is offloaded to the GPU from CPU

GPUs are SIMD Engines Underneath:

Distinguish two models:
